thesis.title: Normative Modification
thesis.thesis: A genuine social fact is one whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change to the fact itself, requiring decision, convention, or recognized reinterpretation, while a coincidental regularity can change by drift without such normative significance.
thesis.argument_sketch: If a community stops counting a symbol as currency, the change is either a deliberate devaluation, a recognized break in convention, or a failed convention; it is not merely a change in behavior. If people stop greeting each other in a certain way, that may be a decline of a norm or just drift; the institutional status depends on whether the population treats it as a modification of a shared practice. Institutions have a public logic of change: they can be amended, suspended, or overruled. Coincidental regularities lack this logic because there is no prior fact to modify. Thus the mark is not behavioral continuity but the possibility of a publicly intelligible normative transition.
thesis.why_new: Most literature focuses on the existence of institutions rather than the distinct epistemic status of their change, drift, and amendment.

objection.objection: The criterion makes the ontological status of a pattern depend on the public narrative attached to its alteration. objection.rationale: If unanswered, the thesis is fatal. The argument confuses a retrospective public story about a pattern with a non-circular mark of its social-ontological status. If actual or recognized public transition is required, it misclassifies ordinary normative change: Humean conventions can arise and dissolve through shifting expectations, Hartian rules can lapse or alter through changed practice and attitudes without formal amendment, and Durkheimian social facts change through social processes rather than decisions. Searle's collective-intentional analysis likewise does not reduce every social change to an explicit act of convention. If merely possible public intelligibility is required, the condition is too weak, because statistical, economic, or behavioral regularities can be publicly discussed as changing while remaining non-social or merely coincidental. The sketch therefore provides a restatement of the distinction, not a discriminating criterion.

# Publicly Intelligible Change and the Ontology of Social Facts

A community may stop counting a certain symbol as currency, stop greeting one another in a familiar way, stop treating a certain office as binding, or stop observing a familiar rule of conduct. In each case the behavior may drift. But the philosophical question is not merely whether the behavior changed; it is what kind of fact changed, if any. A mere regularity in behavior can fade without anything normatively significant having happened. A convention, norm, status, or institutional fact can also change without a vote, a proclamation, or a general moment of public recognition. The task, then, is to distinguish a change in a social fact from a change in a coincidental regularity, without reducing social ontology to behavioral continuity or to the actual narratives people happen to tell about their own practices.

I defend a version of the following thesis: a genuine social fact is one whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change to the fact itself, rather than merely as a change in the behavior that had expressed it. This intelligibility is tied to the possibility of decision, convention, or recognized reinterpretation. A coincidental regularity, by contrast, can change by drift without any such normative transition, because there is no prior shared standard whose content is being modified.

The strongest objection to this view is serious. It says that the criterion makes the ontological status of a pattern depend on the public narrative attached to its alteration. Many genuine social facts—norms, expectations, statuses, and group attitudes—change by unreflective drift, fading practice, or collective reinterpretation that participants do not register as a change to the prior fact. Conversely, any stable regularity that a community tracks can later be narrated as “a change to the fact itself” once it is named. On this objection, the proposed test either presupposes that the prior regularity already has the identity conditions of a social fact, or it fails to discriminate social facts from coincidental regularities.

The objection succeeds against a naïve reading of the criterion. If “publicly intelligible” means “actually narrated by members of the community at the time of change,” then the criterion is too weak and too narrative-dependent. My reply is that the criterion should be understood not as a requirement of actual public narration, but as a structural condition on the fact: a social fact is a pattern whose existence and persistence are partly constituted by a shared normative attitude, and whose alteration would be intelligible, in the community’s own conceptual space, as a modification of a shared standard. Public intelligibility is a modal and normative condition, not a discursive event. It is satisfied when the fact belongs to a public space of reasons, where it can be appealed to, challenged, suspended, revised, or recognized as failed. Coincidental regularities may be tracked, named, and described, but they are not embedded in that second-order normative space.

The essay proceeds in four parts. First, I clarify the distinction between social facts and mere regularities. Second, I explain the criterion of publicly intelligible change. Third, I answer the objection by distinguishing actual public narration from the public logic of change, and by showing how drift can change a social fact without being registered as such. Finally, I show that naming a regularity is not sufficient to make it a social fact, and that the criterion is constitutive rather than circular.

## 1. Social Facts and Mere Regularities

Human behavior contains many regularities. People in a town may eat lunch around noon, stop at a certain point on a road, greet one another with a handshake, keep windows closed during a certain season, or defer to a particular person in a meeting. Some of these regularities are coincidental: they arise from independent causes—weather, hunger, fear, convenience, geography, or habit—and they can fade when those causes change. Others are social facts: they are sustained, at least in part, by shared expectations, commitments, conventions, norms, or institutional roles.

The difference is not that social facts are always more stable than regularities. Conventions can be fragile; coincidental regularities can be extremely persistent. The difference is not that social facts are always intentional, because many social practices are only weakly intentional or are maintained through inherited expectations rather than active planning. Nor is the difference simply that social facts are known by the participants, because many social facts are not fully understood by those who live within them.

The difference lies in the normative structure surrounding the pattern. A mere regularity is a fact about what happens. A social fact is a fact about what happens in a way that is publicly meaningful as a shared reason. When a regularity is a social fact, it has a logic of persistence and change that is not available to a coincidental pattern.

Consider a traffic norm. Drivers in a city stop at red lights. If some drivers begin to run red lights, the norm may still obtain; the drivers are deviating. If everyone begins to proceed through red lights and the community treats this as a change in the rule, then the fact has changed. If the change is only that drivers are tired, distracted, or in a hurry, then the behavior has changed, but the norm may not have. The public question is whether the shared standard has been amended, suspended, overruled, or abandoned. A coincidental regularity does not support that question. If a group of pedestrians happens to cross at a particular spot because of sight lines, and later crosses elsewhere because of a new construction, we may describe the change, but we do not naturally ask whether “the crossing norm” has been violated or amended, unless there is some public standard involved.

This illustrates the point I want to defend. A social fact is not identical to a regularity. It is a regularity that has a normative role in public life: it is treated, at least partly, as a reason for action, as a standard of compliance, or as a shared commitment. Because of that role, the fact has an identity over time that can persist through deviations and can be altered as a whole. A coincidental regularity lacks this normative role. It can be described, predicted, and tracked, but it is not the kind of thing that can be violated, justified, amended, or reinterpreted in a publicly intelligible way.

## 2. Public Intelligibility, Not Public Announcement

The thesis can be stated as follows: a genuine social fact is one whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change to the fact itself. This does not mean that every alteration must be announced, recorded, or recognized by all participants at the moment it occurs. Rather, it means that the fact belongs to a public conceptual space in which its alteration would be intelligible as a change in a shared standard.

A fact has a public logic of change when there is a public way of distinguishing between three cases:

1. The fact continues, though some behavior deviates from it.  
2. The fact changes, is amended, suspended, overruled, or ceases to obtain.  
3. The behavior changes, but no social fact changes because no shared standard was involved.

A social fact has this public logic because it is constituted, at least in part, by a shared normative attitude. That attitude may be a convention, a norm, a status, a role, a group commitment, or an institutional recognition. It is not merely a forecast of what others will do. It is a reason that participants can appeal to, and that can be challenged, revised, or abandoned in a way that is meaningful to the community.

This is why “publicly intelligible” should not be read as “narrated in public.” Publicness here is not the same as publicity in the media sense, or even as collective awareness. It is public in the normative sense that the fact is accessible as a shared reason. A norm can be public even if no one is currently reflecting on it. A convention can be public even if its content is taken for granted. An institutional fact can be public even if its origins are forgotten. What matters is that the fact is the kind of thing that can be appealed to in public reasoning and that can be modified through a public logic of change.

Searle’s account of institutional facts helps clarify the point. Institutional facts depend on constitutive rules of the form “X counts as Y in C.” Money, offices, property, marriages, and legal statuses are not just behavioral regularities; they are facts constituted by shared recognition and constitutive rules. Such facts have a public logic of revision: they can be created, altered, suspended, or abolished through decisions, conventions, or recognized reinterpretations. A coin may cease to be money not only by formal demonetization but by a recognized breakdown in the shared expectation that it functions as money. The important thing is that the fact is not merely a pattern of behavior; it is a pattern that has an institutional role in a public system of reasons (Searle 1995).

A coincidental regularity lacks this structure. It may be stable, shared, and even common knowledge. But it is not constituted by a shared normative attitude that gives it an institutional role. If it changes, the change is not a modification of a shared standard; it is simply the arrival of a different pattern. The language of “altering the fact itself” is, in such cases, at best metaphorical.

## 3. The Strongest Objection

The strongest objection is this: the criterion makes the ontological status of a pattern depend on the public narrative attached to its alteration. Many genuine social facts, especially norms, expectations, statuses, and group attitudes, change by unreflective drift, fading practice, or collective reinterpretation that participants do not register as a change to the prior fact. Conversely, any stable regularity that a community tracks can be publicly narrated as a “change to the fact itself” once it is named. Thus the test either presupposes that the prior regularity already has the identity conditions of a social fact, or it fails to discriminate social facts from coincidental regularities.

This objection has two main parts. The first part says that the criterion is too demanding if it requires actual public recognition: many real changes in social facts are quiet, gradual, and unreflective. The second part says that the criterion is too weak if it only requires the possibility of public narration: almost any regularity can be narrated as a social fact once we attach the right label to it.

I will answer the first part by distinguishing actual public narration from the public logic of change. I will answer the second part by distinguishing descriptive tracking from normative constitution. The reply depends on a precise claim: what makes a fact social is not that it is narrated, but that it is embedded in a shared normative attitude that has a public logic of revision.

## 4. Drift Can Change a Social Fact Without a Public Announcement

The objection is right that many social facts change without anyone saying, “We have now changed the fact.” Norms fade. Conventions loosen. Institutions become obsolete. Statuses become hollow. Collective expectations shift. These changes are often not accompanied by a decision, a formal amendment, or a public declaration. They occur through what Ostrom calls drift, where institutional arrangements change gradually because of changes in context, practice, or belief without a deliberate act of institutional reform (Ostrom 1990).

But drift is not a free-floating third kind of change, alongside decision and recognized reinterpretation. Drift must be analyzed in terms of what is drifting. There are at least three possibilities.

First, the behavior may drift while the normative role persists. People may stop greeting one another with a handshake during a pandemic, or a norm against a certain practice may be less often invoked during a period of social stress. The behavior changes, but the shared standard may still be understood to obtain. The fact has not changed; it is being deviated from, suspended, or merely less actively practiced.

Second, the normative role itself may drift. The shared expectation that a certain practice is required, proper, or binding may weaken. The community may gradually stop treating the practice as a standard, though no one makes a formal decision to abolish it. In that case, the social fact has changed. The change is unreflective, but it is not non-public in the relevant sense. It is public because the fact was constituted by a shared normative attitude, and the alteration is intelligible as a change in that attitude. We can say, retrospectively or prospectively, “The norm has lapsed,” “The convention has become obsolete,” or “We no longer treat that as a binding practice.” That intelligibility does not require that the community has already said those words.

Third, the behavior may drift while no normative role was ever present. A group may habitually eat at the same hour because of work schedules, and later stop doing so because the schedules change. There may be a public description of the change, but there is no shared standard whose modification has occurred. The fact that there was a regularity is a thin descriptive fact; it is not a social fact in the normative or institutional sense.

The important distinction is between drift in behavior and drift in the normative attitude that sustains a social fact. A norm can fade without anyone announcing its death. A convention can become unstable without a formal replacement. A status can lose its force without a legal ruling. None of this undermines the criterion, because the criterion does not require that the change be publicly narrated at the moment it happens. It requires that the fact be the kind of fact whose change would be publicly intelligible as a change in a shared reason.

Bicchieri’s account of social norms helps clarify the point. A social norm is not merely a regularity plus a belief that others are doing it. It involves a combination of empirical expectation—most people do or are expected to do X—normative expectation—most people expect me to do X—and conditional correctness—X is appropriate if others do it (Bicchieri 2017). Changes in any of these components can occur gradually. A norm can fade because the empirical expectation weakens, because the normative expectation weakens, or because the sense of conditional correctness diminishes. These changes may be unreflective. But they are changes in the normative structure, not merely in the behavior. That is why they can be changes in the social fact itself.

This answers the first part of the objection. The criterion is not that every actual transition must be publicly registered. It is that the fact has a public logic of change. A social fact can change by drift, but its drift is drift in the shared normative attitude that constitutes it. The public character of the fact lies in its being a shared reason, not in its being consciously remembered or narrated at every moment.

## 5. Naming a Regularity Is Not Enough

The second part of the objection says that any stable regularity that a community tracks can be publicly narrated as a change to the fact itself once it is named. This is true in a trivial sense. A community can call a pattern “the tradition,” “the custom,” “the way we do things,” or “our rule.” It can later say that this has changed. But naming does not confer normative status. A name can create a descriptive object; it does not create a shared reason.

To see this, distinguish between two kinds of public description. A community can describe a regularity descriptively: “We used to eat lunch at noon, but now we eat later.” It can also describe a normative transition: “The rule used to be that meetings begin at noon, but now they begin later.” The first is a description of changed behavior. The second is a description of a changed standard. The same words—“we used to,” “now we”—can occur in both contexts, but their normative force differs.

A regularity becomes a social fact when it is not merely tracked, but is treated as a reason for action in a public space of accountability. This involves second-order features that a mere regularity lacks. Participants can cite the pattern as a reason. They can criticize deviations. They can justify exceptions. They can suspend the pattern temporarily. They can revise it deliberately. They can recognize that it has been overruled. They can treat its disappearance as a loss, a failure, a reform, or a corruption. These are not infallible markers, because people sometimes speak normatively about things that are not fully normative. But taken together, they indicate that the pattern is embedded in a shared normative attitude.

A coincidental regularity may be tracked and named, but it does not support this second-order logic. If a group habitually crosses a street at a certain point because of geography, and later crosses elsewhere, we can narrate the change. But unless the group treats the crossing point as a shared standard, there is no violation, no amendment, no justification, no public reason of the relevant kind. The fact that a historian later calls the pattern a “custom” does not make it a norm. The fact that a sociologist labels a regularity an “institution” does not make it institutional. Labels are evidence at best; they are not ontologically decisive.

This point answers the converse horn of the objection. Not every stable regularity can be made into a social fact by public narration. Narration can be false, metaphorical, or merely descriptive. A community can say, “Our custom has changed,” even if there was never a custom in the normative sense. What matters is whether the narration tracks a public normative structure. If it does, the pattern was a social fact. If it does not, the pattern was a regularity that has been retrospectively given the appearance of social factuality.

The public narrative is therefore not the ground of the fact’s status. The ground is the shared normative attitude that makes the fact publicly accessible as a reason. The narrative is a possible expression of that attitude, not its substitute.

## 6. The Criterion Does Not Presuppose the Identity Conditions It Is Meant to Explain

The objection also says that the test may be circular. To ask whether a change is publicly intelligible as a change to a social fact, it seems we must already know that the prior regularity was a social fact. But that is precisely what the test is supposed to establish.

This charge rests on a misunderstanding of the criterion. The criterion is not a procedure that begins with an already identified social fact and asks whether its change was public. It is a way of identifying the fact by the normative structure that gives it identity. The prior regularity is a social fact because it is sustained by a shared normative expectation that has a public logic of modification. The expectation is not the fact itself; it is the attitude that makes the fact public and gives it identity conditions.

This is not circular. We can identify normative attitudes without first assuming the social fact they constitute. We look for the second-order features described above: appeal, criticism, justification, exception, suspension, revision, and collective accountability. These are not identical to the fact; they are the public practices through which the fact is expressed and maintained. A convention is not identical to the behavior of following it, though it is expressed in that behavior. A norm is not identical to the expectation that others expect one to comply, though it is sustained by that expectation. A status is not identical to the deference shown to a person, though it is expressed in that deference.

Lewis’s account of conventions is useful here. A convention is not merely a regularity; it is a regularity that solves a coordination problem through common expectations. The behavioral pattern is conventional because it is coordinated around a shared expectation that others will follow it, and because it is normatively operative as a reason for following it (Lewis 1969). The common expectation is not a mere prediction. It is a public reason: I drive on the right because I expect you to drive on the right, and because the expectation is part of a shared solution. If the expectation changes, the convention changes. That change may occur gradually, but it is a change in the social fact because the shared reason has changed.

Searle’s account reinforces the point. Institutional facts are constituted by shared recognition and constitutive rules. The identity of the fact is not exhausted by the behavior that instantiates it. An office can persist despite the misconduct of the office-holder. A currency can persist despite counterfeiting. A norm can persist despite widespread violation. Conversely, an office can be empty, a currency can be demonetized, and a norm can lapse even if some behavior continues. The identity conditions of the fact are supplied by its institutional role, not by the mere continuity of behavior (Searle 1995).

Collective intentionality adds a further dimension. Social facts are often constituted by joint commitments or shared intentions, not merely by parallel individual expectations (Gilbert 2007; Bratman 1999). A group can be committed to a practice, and that commitment can weaken or be revised without a formal meeting. The fact is public because the commitment is a “we”-attitude: it is something the group has, not merely a collection of individual attitudes. Its change is publicly intelligible because it is a change in a shared reason, even if no one explicitly reflects on the change at the time.

Thus the criterion is constitutive rather than circular. It does not ask, after we have identified a social fact, whether its change was public. It asks whether the pattern is embedded in a shared normative attitude that has a public logic of change. That normative attitude supplies the identity conditions of the fact. The fact is the same fact over time when the shared reason is maintained, even if behavior varies. It is a different fact, or a ceased fact, when the shared reason is altered or abandoned.

## 7. Applications and Limits

The criterion clarifies several familiar cases.

### Currency

If a community stops counting a symbol as currency, the change is not merely a change in behavior. The symbol either ceases to count as money because of a decision, because of a recognized break in convention, or because of a gradual failure in the shared expectation that it functions as money. In each case, the alteration is intelligible as a change to the institutional fact. If, by contrast, a group of children stops using paper scraps as pretend money because their play has moved on, no institutional fact has changed unless there was a shared rule or role that made the scraps function as money in a public sense. The behavior changed, but the normative structure did not.

### Greetings

If people stop greeting one another in a certain way, the explanation matters. The change may be a decline of a norm, a temporary suspension, a recognized reinterpretation, or mere drift in behavior. If the greeting had normative force—if deviations were criticized, exceptions justified, and the practice cited as a reason—then its fading can be a change in the social fact. If it was only a pattern produced by mood, fatigue, or changing fashions, then no norm has changed. The public question “Has the greeting norm changed?” is intelligible only in the first case.

### Statuses and Offices

A person may be recognized as a leader, a teacher, a judge, or a representative. The status is a social fact because it is constituted by shared recognition and has a public logic of conferral, revocation, suspension, or failure. If the community stops recognizing the status, the fact changes, even if no formal decision is made. But if a self-styled leader simply loses the attention of a crowd that never treated the leadership as a shared standard, no status fact has changed. The deference was a regularity, not a public recognition.

### Group Attitudes

The objection mentions group attitudes. Some group attitudes are descriptive facts: a population may become less optimistic, more fearful, or less trusting. Such facts can change by drift. But they are not all social facts in the normative or institutional sense at issue here. If a shared attitude has no public normative role—if it is not treated as a shared reason, standard, or commitment—then its change is a change in a descriptive collective state, not a change in a social fact of the kind defended here. If, however, the attitude is a public moral norm, a group commitment, or a shared evaluative standard, then its drift can be a change in a social fact, because the attitude was publicly authoritative. The criterion therefore does not deny that group attitudes can change quietly. It distinguishes those group attitudes that are merely aggregate states from those that are public normative facts.

This limit is important. The thesis is not about every collective fact. It is not about every statistical regularity in a population, every shared belief, or every common mood. It is about those social facts whose existence is partly constituted by public normative relations: conventions, norms, statuses, offices, institutional roles, and group commitments. For these facts, the public logic of change is not an accidental feature; it is part of what makes them what they are.

## 8. Conclusion

The mark of a genuine social fact is not behavioral continuity, nor actual public narration, nor the existence of a name attached to a pattern. It is public normative accountability. A social fact is a pattern that has a shared normative role: it is treated, at least partly, as a reason for action, a standard of compliance, or a public commitment. Because of that role, the fact has an identity over time that can persist through deviations and can be altered through a public logic of change.

Coincidental regularities can also change by drift, but their drift is not a change to a shared standard. There is no prior normative role to modify. A stable regularity may be tracked, named, and described, but unless it is embedded in a shared normative attitude, it remains a mere pattern. The public narrative is not the ground of its social status; at most, it is a possible expression of that status.

The strongest objection is therefore answered by a refinement of the original thesis. The ontological status of a pattern does not depend on the public narrative attached to its alteration. It depends on whether the pattern is constituted by a shared normative attitude whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change in a shared reason. Social facts can change by unreflective drift, but their drift is drift in the public normative structure that makes them social. Coincidental regularities can change by drift, but their drift lacks normative significance because there is no public standard whose modification has occurred. The difference is not whether a story can be told, but whether the fact belongs to a public space of reasons in which its change is intelligible as a change to the fact itself.

rounds.essay_in:
# Publicly Intelligible Change and the Ontology of Social Facts

A community may stop counting a certain symbol as currency, stop greeting one another in a familiar way, stop treating a certain office as binding, or stop observing a familiar rule of conduct. In each case the behavior may drift. But the philosophical question is not merely whether the behavior changed; it is what kind of fact changed, if any. A mere regularity in behavior can fade without anything normatively significant having happened. A convention, norm, status, or institutional fact can also change without a vote, a proclamation, or a general moment of public recognition. The task, then, is to distinguish a change in a social fact from a change in a coincidental regularity, without reducing social ontology to behavioral continuity or to the actual narratives people happen to tell about their own practices.

I defend a version of the following thesis: a genuine social fact is one whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change to the fact itself, rather than merely as a change in the behavior that had expressed it. This intelligibility is tied to the possibility of decision, convention, or recognized reinterpretation. A coincidental regularity, by contrast, can change by drift without any such normative transition, because there is no prior shared standard whose content is being modified.

The strongest objection to this view is serious. It says that the criterion makes the ontological status of a pattern depend on the public narrative attached to its alteration. Many genuine social facts—norms, expectations, statuses, and group attitudes—change by unreflective drift, fading practice, or collective reinterpretation that participants do not register as a change to the prior fact. Conversely, any stable regularity that a community tracks can later be narrated as “a change to the fact itself” once it is named. On this objection, the proposed test either presupposes that the prior regularity already has the identity conditions of a social fact, or it fails to discriminate social facts from coincidental regularities.

The objection succeeds against a naïve reading of the criterion. If “publicly intelligible” means “actually narrated by members of the community at the time of change,” then the criterion is too weak and too narrative-dependent. My reply is that the criterion should be understood not as a requirement of actual public narration, but as a structural condition on the fact: a social fact is a pattern whose existence and persistence are partly constituted by a shared normative attitude, and whose alteration would be intelligible, in the community’s own conceptual space, as a modification of a shared standard. Public intelligibility is a modal and normative condition, not a discursive event. It is satisfied when the fact belongs to a public space of reasons, where it can be appealed to, challenged, suspended, revised, or recognized as failed. Coincidental regularities may be tracked, named, and described, but they are not embedded in that second-order normative space.

The essay proceeds in four main parts, followed by applications and a conclusion. First, I clarify the distinction between social facts and mere regularities. Second, I explain the criterion of publicly intelligible change. Third, I answer the objection by distinguishing actual public narration from the public logic of change, and by showing how drift can change a social fact without being registered as such. Finally, I show that naming a regularity is not sufficient to make it a social fact, and that the criterion is constitutive rather than circular.

## 1. Social Facts and Mere Regularities

Human behavior contains many regularities. People in a town may eat lunch around noon, stop at a certain point on a road, greet one another with a handshake, keep windows closed during a certain season, or defer to a particular person in a meeting. Some of these regularities are coincidental: they arise from independent causes—weather, hunger, fear, convenience, geography, or habit—and they can fade when those causes change. Others are social facts: they are sustained, at least in part, by shared expectations, commitments, conventions, norms, or institutional roles.

The difference is not that social facts are always more stable than regularities. Conventions can be fragile; coincidental regularities can be extremely persistent. The difference is not that social facts are always intentional, because many social practices are only weakly intentional or are maintained through inherited expectations rather than active planning. Nor is the difference simply that social facts are known by the participants, because many social facts are not fully understood by those who live within them.

The difference lies in the normative structure surrounding the pattern. A mere regularity is a fact about what happens. A social fact is a fact about what happens in a way that is publicly meaningful as a shared reason. When a regularity is a social fact, it has a logic of persistence and change that is not available to a coincidental pattern.

Consider a traffic norm. Drivers in a city stop at red lights. If some drivers begin to run red lights, the norm may still obtain; the drivers are deviating. If everyone begins to proceed through red lights and the community treats this as a change in the rule, then the fact has changed. If the change is only that drivers are tired, distracted, or in a hurry, then the behavior has changed, but the norm may not have. The public question is whether the shared standard has been amended, suspended, overruled, or abandoned. A coincidental regularity does not support that question. If a group of pedestrians happens to cross at a particular spot because of sight lines, and later crosses elsewhere because of a new construction, we may describe the change, but we do not naturally ask whether “the crossing norm” has been violated or amended, unless there is some public standard involved.

This illustrates the point I want to defend. A social fact is not identical to a regularity. It is a regularity that has a normative role in public life: it is treated, at least partly, as a reason for action, as a standard of compliance, or as a shared commitment. Because of that role, the fact has an identity over time that can persist through deviations and can be altered as a whole. A coincidental regularity lacks this normative role. It can be described, predicted, and tracked, but it is not the kind of thing that can be violated, justified, amended, or reinterpreted in a publicly intelligible way.

## 2. Public Intelligibility, Not Public Announcement

The thesis can be stated as follows: a genuine social fact is one whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change to the fact itself. This does not mean that every alteration must be announced, recorded, or recognized by all participants at the moment it occurs. Rather, it means that the fact belongs to a public conceptual space in which its alteration would be intelligible as a change in a shared standard.

A fact has a public logic of change when there is a public way of distinguishing between three cases:

1. The fact continues, though some behavior deviates from it.
2. The fact changes, is amended, suspended, overruled, or ceases to obtain.
3. The behavior changes, but no social fact changes because no shared standard was involved.

A social fact has this public logic because it is constituted, at least in part, by a shared normative attitude. That attitude may be a convention, a norm, a status, a role, a group commitment, or an institutional recognition. It is not merely a forecast of what others will do. It is a reason that participants can appeal to, and that can be challenged, revised, or abandoned in a way that is meaningful to the community.

The point is not that any pattern whose history can be sorted into these three categories is thereby a social fact. The public logic must be a logic of shared reasons: the community must be able to treat the pattern as a standard that can be complied with, challenged, or revised. A merely descriptive taxonomy, even a public one, does not by itself confer social factuality.

This is why “publicly intelligible” should not be read as “narrated in public.” Publicness here is not the same as publicity in the media sense, or even as collective awareness. It is public in the normative sense that the fact is accessible as a shared reason. A norm can be public even if no one is currently reflecting on it. A convention can be public even if its content is taken for granted. An institutional fact can be public even if its origins are forgotten. What matters is that the fact is the kind of thing that can be appealed to in public reasoning and that can be modified through a public logic of change.

Searle’s account of institutional facts helps clarify the point. Institutional facts depend on constitutive rules of the form “X counts as Y in C.” Money, offices, property, marriages, and legal statuses are not just behavioral regularities; they are facts constituted by shared recognition and constitutive rules. Such facts have a public logic of revision: they can be created, altered, suspended, or abolished through decisions, conventions, or recognized reinterpretations. A coin may cease to be money not only by formal demonetization but by a recognized breakdown in the shared expectation that it functions as money. The important thing is that the fact is not merely a pattern of behavior; it is a pattern that has an institutional role in a public system of reasons (Searle 1995).

A coincidental regularity lacks this structure. It may be stable, shared, and even common knowledge. But it is not constituted by a shared normative attitude that gives it an institutional role. If it changes, the change is not a modification of a shared standard; it is simply the arrival of a different pattern. The language of “altering the fact itself” is, in such cases, at best metaphorical.

## 3. The Strongest Objection

The strongest objection is this: the criterion makes the ontological status of a pattern depend on the public narrative attached to its alteration. Many genuine social facts, especially norms, expectations, statuses, and group attitudes, change by unreflective drift, fading practice, or collective reinterpretation that participants do not register as a change to the prior fact. Conversely, any stable regularity that a community tracks can be publicly narrated as a “change to the fact itself” once it is named. Thus the test either presupposes that the prior regularity already has the identity conditions of a social fact, or it fails to discriminate social facts from coincidental regularities.

This objection has two main parts. The first part says that the criterion is too demanding if it requires actual public recognition: many real changes in social facts are quiet, gradual, and unreflective. The second part says that the criterion is too weak if it only requires the possibility of public narration: almost any regularity can be narrated as a social fact once we attach the right label to it.

I will answer the first part by distinguishing actual public narration from the public logic of change. I will answer the second part by distinguishing descriptive tracking from normative constitution. The reply depends on a precise claim: what makes a fact social is not that it is narrated, but that it is embedded in a shared normative attitude that has a public logic of revision.

## 4. Drift Can Change a Social Fact Without a Public Announcement

The objection is right that many social facts change without anyone saying, “We have now changed the fact.” Norms fade. Conventions loosen. Institutions become obsolete. Statuses become hollow. Collective expectations shift. These changes are often not accompanied by a decision, a formal amendment, or a public declaration. They occur through what Ostrom calls drift, where institutional arrangements change gradually because of changes in context, practice, or belief without a deliberate act of institutional reform (Ostrom 1990).

But drift is not a free-floating third kind of change, alongside decision and recognized reinterpretation. Drift must be analyzed in terms of what is drifting. There are at least three possibilities.

First, the behavior may drift while the normative role persists. People may stop greeting one another with a handshake during a pandemic, or a norm against a certain practice may be less often invoked during a period of social stress. The behavior changes, but the shared standard may still be understood to obtain. The fact has not changed; it is being deviated from, suspended, or merely less actively practiced.

Second, the normative role itself may drift. The shared expectation that a certain practice is required, proper, or binding may weaken. The community may gradually stop treating the practice as a standard, though no one makes a formal decision to abolish it. In that case, the social fact has changed. The change is unreflective, but it is not non-public in the relevant sense. It is public because the fact was constituted by a shared normative attitude, and the alteration is intelligible as a change in that attitude. We can say, retrospectively or prospectively, “The norm has lapsed,” “The convention has become obsolete,” or “We no longer treat that as a binding practice.” That intelligibility does not require that the community has already said those words.

Third, the behavior may drift while no normative role was ever present. A group may habitually eat at the same hour because of work schedules, and later stop doing so because the schedules change. There may be a public description of the change, but there is no shared standard whose modification has occurred. The fact that there was a regularity is a thin descriptive fact; it is not a social fact in the normative or institutional sense.

The important distinction is between drift in behavior and drift in the normative attitude that sustains a social fact. A norm can fade without anyone announcing its death. A convention can become unstable without a formal replacement. A status can lose its force without a legal ruling. None of this undermines the criterion, because the criterion does not require that the change be publicly narrated at the moment it happens. It requires that the fact be the kind of fact whose change would be publicly intelligible as a change in a shared reason.

Bicchieri’s account of social norms helps clarify the point. A social norm is not merely a regularity plus a belief that others are doing it. It involves a combination of empirical expectation—most people do or are expected to do X—normative expectation—most people expect me to do X—and conditional correctness—X is appropriate if others do it (Bicchieri 2017). Changes in any of these components can occur gradually. A norm can fade because the empirical expectation weakens, because the normative expectation weakens, or because the sense of conditional correctness diminishes. These changes may be unreflective. But they are changes in the normative structure, not merely in the behavior. That is why they can be changes in the social fact itself.

This answers the first part of the objection. The criterion is not that every actual transition must be publicly registered. It is that the fact has a public logic of change. A social fact can change by drift, but its drift is drift in the shared normative attitude that constitutes it. The public character of the fact lies in its being a shared reason, not in its being consciously remembered or narrated at every moment.

## 5. Naming a Regularity Is Not Enough

The second part of the objection says that any stable regularity that a community tracks can be publicly narrated as a change to the fact itself once it is named. This is true in a trivial sense. A community can call a pattern “the tradition,” “the custom,” “the way we do things,” or “our rule.” It can later say that this has changed. But naming does not confer normative status. A name can create a descriptive object; it does not create a shared reason.

To see this, distinguish between two kinds of public description. A community can describe a regularity descriptively: “We used to eat lunch at noon, but now we eat later.” It can also describe a normative transition: “The rule used to be that meetings begin at noon, but now they begin later.” The first is a description of changed behavior. The second is a description of a changed standard. The same words—“we used to,” “now we”—can occur in both contexts, but their normative force differs.

A regularity becomes a social fact when it is not merely tracked, but is treated as a reason for action in a public space of accountability. This involves second-order features that a mere regularity lacks. Participants can cite the pattern as a reason. They can criticize deviations. They can justify exceptions. They can suspend the pattern temporarily. They can revise it deliberately. They can recognize that it has been overruled. They can treat its disappearance as a loss, a failure, a reform, or a corruption. These are not infallible markers, because people sometimes speak normatively about things that are not fully normative. But taken together, they indicate that the pattern is embedded in a shared normative attitude.

A coincidental regularity may be tracked and named, but it does not support this second-order logic. If a group habitually crosses a street at a certain point because of geography, and later crosses elsewhere, we can narrate the change. But unless the group treats the crossing point as a shared standard, there is no violation, no amendment, no justification, no public reason of the relevant kind. The fact that a historian later calls the pattern a “custom” does not make it a norm. The fact that a sociologist labels a regularity an “institution” does not make it institutional. Labels are evidence at best; they are not ontologically decisive.

This point answers the converse horn of the objection. Not every stable regularity can be made into a social fact by public narration. Narration can be false, metaphorical, or merely descriptive. A community can say, “Our custom has changed,” even if there was never a custom in the normative sense. What matters is whether the narration tracks a public normative structure. If it does, the pattern was a social fact. If it does not, the pattern was a regularity that has been retrospectively given the appearance of social factuality.

The public narrative is therefore not the ground of the fact’s status. The ground is the shared normative attitude that makes the fact publicly accessible as a reason. The narrative is a possible expression of that attitude, not its substitute.

## 6. The Criterion Does Not Presuppose the Identity Conditions It Is Meant to Explain

The objection also says that the test may be circular. To ask whether a change is publicly intelligible as a change to a social fact, it seems we must already know that the prior regularity was a social fact. But that is precisely what the test is supposed to establish.

This charge rests on a misunderstanding of the criterion. The criterion is not a procedure that begins with an already identified social fact and asks whether its change was public. It is a way of identifying the fact by the normative structure that gives it identity. The prior regularity is a social fact because it is sustained by a shared normative expectation that has a public logic of modification. The expectation is not the fact itself; it is the attitude that makes the fact public and gives it identity conditions.

This is not circular. We can identify normative attitudes without first assuming the social fact they constitute. We look for the second-order features described above: appeal, criticism, justification, exception, suspension, revision, and collective accountability. These are not identical to the fact; they are the public practices through which the fact is expressed and maintained. A convention is not identical to the behavior of following it, though it is expressed in that behavior. A norm is not identical to the expectation that others expect one to comply, though it is sustained by that expectation. A status is not identical to the deference shown to a person, though it is expressed in that deference.

Lewis’s account of conventions is useful here. A convention is not merely a regularity; it is a regularity that solves a coordination problem through common expectations. The behavioral pattern is conventional because it is coordinated around a shared expectation that others will follow it, and because it is normatively operative as a reason for following it (Lewis 1969). The common expectation is not a mere prediction. It is a public reason: I drive on the right because I expect you to drive on the right, and because the expectation is part of a shared solution. If the expectation changes, the convention changes. That change may occur gradually, but it is a change in the social fact because the shared reason has changed.

Searle’s account reinforces the point. Institutional facts are constituted by shared recognition and constitutive rules. The identity of the fact is not exhausted by the behavior that instantiates it. An office can persist despite the misconduct of the office-holder. A currency can persist despite counterfeiting. A norm can persist despite widespread violation. Conversely, an office can be empty, a currency can be demonetized, and a norm can lapse even if some behavior continues. The identity conditions of the fact are supplied by its institutional role, not by the mere continuity of behavior (Searle 1995).

Collective intentionality adds a further dimension. Social facts are often constituted by joint commitments or shared intentions, not merely by parallel individual expectations (Gilbert 2007; Bratman 1999). A group can be committed to a practice, and that commitment can weaken or be revised without a formal meeting. The fact is public because the commitment is a “we”-attitude: it is something the group has, not merely a collection of individual attitudes. Its change is publicly intelligible because it is a change in a shared reason, even if no one explicitly reflects on the change at the time.

Thus the criterion is constitutive rather than circular. It does not ask, after we have identified a social fact, whether its change was public. It asks whether the pattern is embedded in a shared normative attitude that has a public logic of change. That normative attitude supplies the identity conditions of the fact. The fact is the same fact over time when the shared reason is maintained, even if behavior varies. It is a different fact, or a ceased fact, when the shared reason is altered or abandoned.

## 7. Applications and Limits

The criterion clarifies several familiar cases.

### Currency

If a community stops counting a symbol as currency, the change is not merely a change in behavior. The symbol either ceases to count as money because of a decision, because of a recognized break in convention, or because of a gradual failure in the shared expectation that it functions as money. In each case, the alteration is intelligible as a change to the institutional fact. If, by contrast, a group of children stops using paper scraps as pretend money because their play has moved on, no institutional fact has changed unless there was a shared rule or role that made the scraps function as money in a public sense. The behavior changed, but the normative structure did not.

### Greetings

If people stop greeting one another in a certain way, the explanation matters. The change may be a decline of a norm, a temporary suspension, a recognized reinterpretation, or mere drift in behavior. If the greeting had normative force—if deviations were criticized, exceptions justified, and the practice cited as a reason—then its fading can be a change in the social fact. If it was only a pattern produced by mood, fatigue, or changing fashions, then no norm has changed. The public question “Has the greeting norm changed?” is intelligible only in the first case.

### Statuses and Offices

A person may be recognized as a leader, a teacher, a judge, or a representative. The status is a social fact because it is constituted by shared recognition and has a public logic of conferral, revocation, suspension, or failure. If the community stops recognizing the status, the fact changes, even if no formal decision is made. But if a self-styled leader simply loses the attention of a crowd that never treated the leadership as a shared standard, no status fact has changed. The deference was a regularity, not a public recognition.

### Group Attitudes

The objection mentions group attitudes. Some group attitudes are descriptive facts: a population may become less optimistic, more fearful, or less trusting. Such facts can change by drift. But they are not all social facts in the normative or institutional sense at issue here. If a shared attitude has no public normative role—if it is not treated as a shared reason, standard, or commitment—then its change is a change in a descriptive collective state, not a change in a social fact of the kind defended here. If, however, the attitude is a public moral norm, a group commitment, or a shared evaluative standard, then its drift can be a change in a social fact, because the attitude was publicly authoritative. The criterion therefore does not deny that group attitudes can change quietly. It distinguishes those group attitudes that are merely aggregate states from those that are public normative facts.

This limit is important. The thesis is not about every collective fact. It is not about every statistical regularity in a population, every shared belief, or every common mood. It is about those social facts whose existence is partly constituted by public normative relations: conventions, norms, statuses, offices, institutional roles, and group commitments. For these facts, the public logic of change is not an accidental feature; it is part of what makes them what they are.

## 8. Conclusion

The mark of a genuine social fact is not behavioral continuity, nor actual public narration, nor the existence of a name attached to a pattern. It is public normative accountability. A social fact is a pattern that has a shared normative role: it is treated, at least partly, as a reason for action, a standard of compliance, or a public commitment. Because of that role, the fact has an identity over time that can persist through deviations and can be altered through a public logic of change.

Coincidental regularities can also change by drift, but their drift is not a change to a shared standard. There is no prior normative role to modify. A stable regularity may be tracked, named, and described, but unless it is embedded in a shared normative attitude, it remains a mere pattern. The public narrative is not the ground of its social status; at most, it is a possible expression of that status.

The strongest objection is therefore answered by a refinement of the original thesis. The ontological status of a pattern does not depend on the public narrative attached to its alteration. It depends on whether the pattern is constituted by a shared normative attitude whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change in a shared reason. Social facts can change by unreflective drift, but their drift is drift in the public normative structure that makes them social. Coincidental regularities can change by drift, but their drift lacks normative significance because there is no public standard whose modification has occurred. The difference is not whether a story can be told, but whether the fact belongs to a public space of reasons in which its change is intelligible as a change to the fact itself.

final.essay:
# Publicly Intelligible Change and the Ontology of Social Facts

A community may stop counting a symbol as currency, stop using a greeting, stop treating an office as binding, or stop observing a rule. The behavior may drift. The question is not whether behavior changed, but what kind of fact changed, if any. A coincidental regularity can fade without anything normatively significant having happened. A convention, norm, status, or institutional fact can also change without a vote, proclamation, or public recognition. The task is to distinguish changes in social facts from changes in mere regularities, without reducing social ontology to behavioral continuity or to participants’ narratives.

I defend: a genuine social fact is one whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change to the fact itself, rather than merely as a change in the behavior that expressed it. This intelligibility is tied to decision, convention, or recognized reinterpretation. A coincidental regularity can change by drift without any normative transition, because there is no prior shared standard whose content is modified.

The strongest objection is that the criterion makes ontological status depend on public narrative. Many social facts change by unreflective drift; conversely, any tracked regularity can later be narrated as a changed fact. The test therefore either presupposes the identity conditions of social facts or fails to discriminate them from regularities. My reply is that public intelligibility is not actual narration. It is a modal and normative condition: a social fact belongs to a public space of reasons, where it can be appealed to, challenged, suspended, revised, or recognized as failed.

## 1. Social Facts and Mere Regularities

Behavior contains many regularities: noon lunches, stopping points, handshakes, closed windows, deference in meetings. Some are coincidental, caused by weather, hunger, convenience, or habit. Others are social facts, sustained partly by shared expectations, commitments, conventions, norms, or institutional roles.

The difference is not stability or intention. Conventions can be fragile; coincidental regularities can be persistent. Social facts are not always fully understood or actively intended. The difference is normative structure. A mere regularity is a fact about what happens. A social fact is a fact about what happens as a publicly meaningful shared reason. It has a logic of persistence and change unavailable to coincidental patterns.

Consider drivers stopping at red lights. If some run red lights, the norm may persist; they deviate. If everyone proceeds and the community treats this as a changed rule, the fact has changed. If the change is only fatigue or hurry, behavior changes but the norm may not. The public question is whether the shared standard has been amended, suspended, overruled, or abandoned. A coincidental regularity does not support that question. A social fact is therefore a regularity with a normative role in public life: treated partly as a reason, standard, or commitment. It can persist through deviations and be altered as a whole. A coincidental regularity lacks this role; it can be described, predicted, and tracked, but not violated, justified, amended, or reinterpreted in a publicly intelligible way.

## 2. Public Intelligibility, Not Public Announcement

The thesis is: a genuine social fact is one whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change to the fact itself. This does not require announcement, recording, or recognition at the moment. It requires that the fact belongs to a public conceptual space in which its alteration would be intelligible as a change in a shared standard.

A fact has a public logic of change when there is a public way to distinguish: 1. the fact continues though behavior deviates; 2. the fact changes, is amended, suspended, overruled, or ceases; 3. behavior changes but no social fact changes because no shared standard was involved. A social fact has this logic because it is constituted partly by a shared normative attitude: a convention, norm, status, role, group commitment, or institutional recognition. This attitude is not merely a forecast. It is a reason participants can appeal to and challenge.

The point is not that any pattern sortable into these categories is a social fact. The public logic must be a logic of shared reasons. A descriptive taxonomy, even a public one, does not confer social factuality. ‘Publicly intelligible’ is not ‘narrated in public.’ Publicness is normative accessibility, not media publicity or collective awareness. A norm can be public though no one is currently reflecting on it. A convention can be public though taken for granted. An institutional fact can be public though its origins are forgotten. What matters is that the fact can be appealed to in public reasoning and modified through a public logic of change.

Searle’s institutional facts clarify this. They depend on constitutive rules of the form ‘X counts as Y in C.’ Money, offices, property, marriages, and legal statuses are not just behavioral patterns; they are constituted by shared recognition and constitutive rules. They can be created, altered, suspended, or abolished through decisions, conventions, or recognized reinterpretations. A coin may cease to be money by formal demonetization or by a recognized breakdown in the shared expectation that it functions as money. The important point is that the fact has an institutional role in a public system of reasons (Searle 1995). A coincidental regularity lacks this structure. If it changes, the change is not a modification of a shared standard; it is simply a different pattern. The language of altering the fact itself is at best metaphorical.

## 3. The Strongest Objection

The objection has two parts. First, the criterion is too demanding if it requires actual public recognition, because many changes in norms, expectations, statuses, and group attitudes are quiet, gradual, and unreflective. Second, the criterion is too weak if it only requires the possibility of public narration, because any stable regularity can be named and narrated as a social fact. The reply distinguishes actual public narration from the public logic of change, and descriptive tracking from normative constitution. What makes a fact social is not that it is narrated, but that it is embedded in a shared normative attitude with a public logic of revision.

## 4. Drift Can Change a Social Fact Without Public Announcement

Many social facts change without anyone saying, ‘We have now changed the fact.’ Norms fade, conventions loosen, institutions become obsolete, statuses become hollow, expectations shift. These changes are often not accompanied by decision, formal amendment, or public declaration. They occur through what Ostrom calls drift: institutional arrangements change gradually through changes in context, practice, or belief without deliberate reform (Ostrom 1990).

Drift must be analyzed by asking what is drifting. Three cases matter. First, behavior drifts while the normative role persists. People may stop handshaking during a pandemic, or a norm may be less often invoked during stress. Behavior changes, but the shared standard may still be understood to obtain. The fact has not changed; it is being deviated from, suspended, or less actively practiced.

Second, the normative role itself drifts. The shared expectation that a practice is required, proper, or binding weakens. The community gradually stops treating it as a standard, though no formal decision abolishes it. Then the social fact has changed. The change is unreflective, but not non-public in the relevant sense. It is public because the fact was constituted by a shared normative attitude, and the alteration is intelligible as a change in that attitude. We can say retrospectively, ‘The norm has lapsed’ or ‘The convention has become obsolete,’ without requiring that the community has already said those words.

Third, behavior drifts while no normative role was ever present. A group may eat at the same hour because of work schedules and later stop when schedules change. There may be a public description, but no shared standard has been modified. The regularity was a thin descriptive fact, not a social fact in the normative or institutional sense. The distinction is between drift in behavior and drift in the normative attitude that sustains a social fact. None undermines the criterion, which does not require public narration at the moment. It requires that the fact be the kind whose change would be publicly intelligible as a change in a shared reason.

Bicchieri’s account of social norms helps. A social norm involves empirical expectation, normative expectation, and conditional correctness: most people do X, most people expect me to do X, and X is appropriate if others do it (Bicchieri 2017). Changes in any component can be gradual. A norm can fade as expectations weaken or conditional correctness diminishes. These may be unreflective, but they are changes in the normative structure, not merely behavior. That is why they can be changes in the social fact itself.

## 5. Naming a Regularity Is Not Enough

Any stable regularity can be named and later narrated as changed. A community can call a pattern ‘the custom’ or ‘our way’ and later say it changed. But naming does not confer normative status. A name can create a descriptive object; it does not create a shared reason.

Distinguish descriptive public description from normative public description. A community can say, ‘We used to eat lunch at noon, but now we eat later.’ This describes changed behavior. It can also say, ‘The rule used to be that meetings begin at noon, but now they begin later.’ This describes a changed standard. The same temporal language can occur in both, but their normative force differs.

A regularity becomes a social fact when it is treated as a reason for action in a public space of accountability. Participants can cite it as a reason, criticize deviations, justify exceptions, suspend it temporarily, revise it deliberately, recognize that it has been overruled, and treat its disappearance as loss, failure, reform, or corruption. These markers are not infallible, but taken together they indicate a shared normative attitude.

A coincidental regularity may be tracked and named, but it does not support this second-order logic. If a group crosses at a point because of geography and later elsewhere, we can narrate the change. Unless the group treats the crossing point as a shared standard, there is no violation, amendment, justification, or relevant public reason. A historian calling it a custom does not make it a norm; a sociologist labeling it an institution does not make it institutional. Narration can be false, metaphorical, or merely descriptive. A community can say, ‘Our custom has changed,’ even if there was never a custom in the normative sense. What matters is whether the narration tracks a public normative structure.

## 6. The Criterion Is Constitutive, Not Circular

The objection may say the test is circular: to ask whether a change is publicly intelligible as a change to a social fact, we must already know the prior regularity was a social fact. But the criterion is not a procedure applied after identifying a social fact. It identifies the fact by the normative structure that gives it identity. The prior regularity is a social fact because it is sustained by a shared normative expectation with a public logic of modification. The expectation is not the fact itself; it is the attitude that makes the fact public and supplies its identity conditions.

This is not circular. We can identify normative attitudes without first assuming the social fact they constitute. We look for second-order features: appeal, criticism, justification, exception, suspension, revision, and collective accountability. These are public practices through which the fact is expressed and maintained. A convention is not identical to the behavior of following it, though it is expressed there. A norm is not identical to the expectation that others expect compliance, though it is sustained there. A status is not identical to deference, though it may be expressed there.

Lewis’s conventions help. A convention is not merely a regularity; it is a regularity that solves a coordination problem through common expectations. The pattern is conventional because it is coordinated around a shared expectation that others will follow it and because it is normatively operative as a reason for following it (Lewis 1969). The expectation is not a mere prediction; it is a public reason. If it changes, the convention changes, even gradually, because the shared reason has changed.

Searle’s institutional facts reinforce this. Institutional facts are constituted by shared recognition and constitutive rules. Their identity is not exhausted by behavior. An office can persist despite misconduct; a currency can persist despite counterfeiting; a norm can persist despite violation. Conversely, an office can be empty, a currency demonetized, or a norm lapsed even if some behavior continues. The identity conditions are supplied by institutional role, not behavioral continuity (Searle 1995).

Collective intentionality adds a further dimension. Social facts are often constituted by joint commitments or shared intentions, not merely parallel individual expectations (Gilbert 2007; Bratman 1999). A group can be committed to a practice, and that commitment can weaken or be revised without a formal meeting. The fact is public because the commitment is a ‘we’-attitude: something the group has, not merely a collection of individual attitudes. Its change is publicly intelligible because it is a change in a shared reason.

Thus the criterion is constitutive rather than circular. It asks whether the pattern is embedded in a shared normative attitude with a public logic of change. That attitude supplies the fact’s identity conditions. The fact persists when the shared reason is maintained, even if behavior varies. It changes or ceases when the shared reason is altered or abandoned.

## 7. Applications and Limits

Currency: If a community stops counting a symbol as currency, the change is not merely behavioral. The symbol either ceases to count as money by decision, by recognized break in convention, or by gradual failure in the shared expectation that it functions as money. In each case, the alteration is intelligible as a change to an institutional fact. If children stop using paper scraps as pretend money because play moves on, no institutional fact changes unless there was a shared rule or role giving the scraps a public monetary function.

Greetings: If people stop greeting in a certain way, the explanation matters. The change may be a decline of a norm, temporary suspension, recognized reinterpretation, or mere behavioral drift. If the greeting had normative force—deviations criticized, exceptions justified, practice cited as a reason—its fading can be a change in the social fact. If it was only a pattern produced by mood, fatigue, or fashion, no norm has changed. The question ‘Has the greeting norm changed?’ is intelligible only in the first case.

Statuses and Offices: A person may be recognized as a leader, teacher, judge, or representative. The status is a social fact because it is constituted by shared recognition, not by individual deference alone, and because it has a public logic of conferral, revocation, suspension, or failure. If the community stops recognizing the status, the fact changes, even without formal decision. But if a self-styled leader merely loses the attention of a crowd that never treated the leadership as a shared standard, no status fact has changed. What was present was a behavioral regularity, not a publicly recognized role; the deference lacked the shared normative attitude that makes a role publicly accountable.

Group Attitudes: Some group attitudes are descriptive collective states: a population may become less optimistic, more fearful, or less trusting. Such facts can change by drift. But they are not all social facts in the normative or institutional sense. If a shared attitude has no public normative role—if it is not treated as a shared reason, standard, or commitment—then its change is not a change in the kind of social fact defended here. If the attitude is a public moral norm, group commitment, or shared evaluative standard, then its drift can change a social fact, because it was publicly authoritative. The criterion distinguishes aggregate states from public normative facts.

The thesis is not about every collective fact, statistical regularity, shared belief, or common mood. It is about those social facts whose existence is partly constituted by public normative relations: conventions, norms, statuses, offices, institutional roles, and group commitments. For these facts, the public logic of change is not accidental; it is part of what makes them what they are.

## 8. Conclusion

The mark of a genuine social fact is not behavioral continuity, actual public narration, or the existence of a name. It is public normative accountability. A social fact is a pattern with a shared normative role: treated partly as a reason, standard, or commitment. Because of that role, it has an identity over time that can persist through deviations and be altered through a public logic of change.

Coincidental regularities can change by drift, but their drift is not a change to a shared standard. There is no prior normative role to modify. A stable regularity may be tracked, named, and described, but unless it is embedded in a shared normative attitude, it remains a mere pattern. The public narrative is not the ground of social status; at most, it is a possible expression of that status.

The strongest objection is answered by refinement. Ontological status does not depend on the public narrative attached to alteration. It depends on whether the pattern is constituted by a shared normative attitude whose alteration is publicly intelligible as a change in a shared reason. Social facts can change by unreflective drift, but their drift is drift in the public normative structure that makes them social. Coincidental regularities can change by drift, but their drift lacks normative significance because there is no public standard whose modification has occurred. The difference is not whether a story can be told, but whether the fact belongs to a public space of reasons in which its change is intelligible as a change to the fact itself.
